newsitem.title: USA: Food needs in developing world seen doubling.
newsitem.headline: Food needs in developing world seen doubling.

text.p: Food needs in developing countries could almost double in the next 30 years and more research must be focused on increasing food production in those needy areas, international experts said in remarks to be delivered Monday at a key U.S. agricultural conference.

Alex McCalla, director of The World Bank's Agriculture and Natural Resources Department, said most of the next 30 year's growth in population will occur in developing nations, and that these regions will rely more and more heavily on imported agricultural products.

To fill the expected big demand, McCalla and other experts speaking at the U.S. Agriculture Department's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum said that growth in food production in the long term must come primarily from better yields, not from area expansion or intensification.

Per Pinstrup-Andersen, director general of the International Food Policy Reserach Institute (IFPRI), urged that agricultural research place a higher priority on increasing productivity in low-income developing countries, not just the well-financed, developed food producing nations.

"The balance between less-favoured and more-favoured areas must be redressed... Much more attention must be directed to the development of appropriate technology for the less-favoured areas," said Pinstrup-Andersen in prepared remarks.
He said accelerated research is needed to develop crops more tolerant of droughts and better suited to fragile soils.

Pinstrup-Andersen pointed to agricultural biotechnology as one of the most promising developments in modern science, but warned that biotechnology research must not be done only in industrialised countries but also has to focus on the needs of farmers in developing nations.
He scolded the "nonpoor" who are critical of biotechnology, and said countries need to develop regulations that ensure safety, but do not cripple new development.
"We cannot afford to be philosophical or elitist about any possible solution, including agricultural biotechnology," he said.
The World Bank's McCalla said economic projections generally point to sufficient global food supplies at least until 2010.

During the years 2010 to 2015, harvested acreage could increase slightly, grain demand is projected to grow more slowly, and grain trade will likely increase. Real grain prices are likely to remain constant or decline. During that time, regional food problems are expected to persist in South Asia and especially in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The longer term outlook from 2020 to 2025, according to IFPRI, show grain prices falling by 20 percent from 1990 and meat prices dropping by 10 percent. Trade should expand significantly, with imports by developing countries doubling. Food problems in Sub-Saharan Africa could cause imports to triple.
IFPRI has predicted global demand for cereals to increase by 55 percent between 1990 and 2020 and demand for livestock products to jump 75 percent.
Pinstrup-Andersen said that in developing nations alone, cereal demand will increase 80 percent and livestock demand by 140 percent.
